axes.name: channel of the act
axes.definition: One side names an act carried out in language — saying, asking, telling, reporting, writing, vocalising; the other names an act carried out with the body or on an object. The single most-proposed axis: all sixteen readers proposed it, ~350 relations.

axes.name: locus of the event
axes.definition: One side names something happening inside the subject — feeling, wanting, believing, noticing, realising, taking a stance; the other names something done or expressed visibly in the world. Where a reader lumps speech together with mental events against the physical, the relation belongs on act_channel, not here.

axes.name: event continuity
axes.pole_y: a separate or subsequent event begun
axes.definition: One side stays inside the act the frame has already set in motion — elaborating, repeating, finishing, handling the same object further; the other breaks off into a distinct act, a new participant, or the next scene. Second-largest axis, proposed by fifteen readers (~300 relations).
merged_from: s7:relation to the act already underway
s9:event continuity: same event vs new event

axes.name: aspectual phase
axes.definition: Both sides concern one event's own timeline: one marks its beginning or its still-running middle, the other its finishing, stopping or closing off. Distinct from event_continuity, which is about same-event versus different-event, not about where in a single event the continuation lands.

axes.name: act versus its outcome
axes.definition: One side names what is done or tried; the other names what the doing produced — the damage, the discovery, the verdict, the state the situation is left in, or the goal it aimed at.

axes.name: dynamicity
axes.definition: One side names something that happens and moves the world; the other names a condition, quality, posture or disposition that simply holds. Distinct from act_vs_outcome: the state here need not be the product of the act named in the frame.

axes.name: lexical weight of the filler
axes.pole_x: content word naming an act or entity
axes.definition: One side supplies a contentful verb or noun that introduces new event material; the other supplies a connective, temporal adverb, particle, existential, filler or semantically light verb that links, times or frames the clause without naming anything. Proposed by all sixteen readers (~190 relations).

axes.name: manner and degree specification
axes.pole_x: specifies how, how much, or in what manner
axes.pole_y: names the act or entity itself, unqualified
axes.definition: One side qualifies an event — its manner, means, speed, care, direction or degree, whether by a manner-specific verb or by an adverb, degree word, negator or evaluative modifier; the other names the act, event or entity being qualified, plainly or generically.

axes.name: entity versus event
axes.definition: The blank is filled on one side by a noun naming who or what is involved, and on the other by a verb or predicate naming what happens. A content contrast, not a grammaticality one — for whether the word can stand in the slot at all, see syntactic_form_fit.

axes.name: fit of the form to the slot
axes.pole_x: stands in the slot as it is
axes.pole_y: needs a different form or further material
axes.definition: A grammatical rather than semantic contrast: one side's word completes the frame bare and finite as given, the other requires an auxiliary, particle, complement, participle, inflection or a change of clause type before it will sit there.

axes.name: argument structure
axes.definition: One side's verbs require or imply a direct object, recipient or complement; the other's stand alone, describe the subject's own motion or state, or continue without one. Independent of what the verb means.

axes.name: target of the act
axes.pole_x: aimed at a person or body
axes.pole_y: aimed at an object, place, document or situation
axes.definition: The kind of act is not what separates the groups — what differs is which entity in the scene the continuation lands on. Covers animacy of the target, which of two salient entities is engaged, and whether the scene's salient object is taken up at all.

axes.name: orientation between the parties
axes.pole_x: self-directed or one party's own side
axes.pole_y: other-directed, shared with or inflicted by another party
axes.definition: One side keeps the act with the subject — their own state, body, situation or course; the other reaches out to, benefits, or is imposed by a second party. Distinct from target_of_act, which contrasts animate with inanimate targets rather than self with other.

axes.name: force of handling
axes.definition: Both sides act on the same scene or object and differ in the violence, impact or abruptness of the handling. About the manner of force, not its consequences — whether anything is damaged belongs on harm_lethality.
merged_from: s7:force and charge of the act

axes.name: harm
axes.definition: One side names an act that wounds, destroys or takes a life, or a state that damages; the other uses, handles, preserves or restores without injury. Degree-of-harm contrasts (wounding versus killing) sit here too.

axes.name: explicitness of the charged term
axes.pole_x: blunt, anatomically explicit, sexual or profane
axes.definition: Both sides fill the same slot and differ in how directly the taboo referent is named — an explicit sexual, anatomical or profane term against a euphemism, circumlocution or non-sexual counterpart.

axes.name: institutional versus personal recourse
axes.pole_x: routed through an institution or formal procedure
axes.definition: One side names a measure carried out through legal, managerial, official or third-party channels; the other names what the person does immediately and on their own.

axes.name: domain specificity
axes.pole_x: belongs to the scene's particular practice or script
axes.definition: One side names an act or term belonging to a bounded practice — cooking, medicine, liturgy, maintenance, a rite, the instrument already in play; the other is everyday vocabulary that would continue almost any frame. Distinct from institutional_register, which is about routing an act through an institution rather than about marked domain vocabulary.

axes.name: deliberation versus execution
axes.pole_x: deliberating, weighing, wanting or taking a stance
axes.definition: One side frames the situation as something to be considered, needed, hedged, consulted about or held a position on; the other names a definite act performed in response to it.

axes.name: illocutionary force
axes.definition: Both sides are utterances or framings, and they differ in what the utterance does — asking how to proceed, ordering, warning, doubting, against asserting, reporting or stating outright.

axes.name: locomotion
axes.definition: One side moves a participant along a path — going, leaving, arriving, fleeing, a manner or direction of motion; the other perceives, handles, transacts or stays put without displacement.

axes.name: disposition of the object
axes.pole_x: object moved, placed or handed on
axes.pole_y: object kept, handled in situ, or no object moved
axes.definition: One side changes an object's location or holder — giving, sending, throwing, placing, transferring, acquiring; the other retains it, works on it where it is, or moves only the agent's own body. Self-motion falls on the second pole because no object changes hands.

axes.name: volition
axes.definition: One side names something the subject chooses and controls; the other something that happens to them, bursts out of them, or is imposed on them — a reflex, an outcome received, a necessity suffered.

axes.name: engagement with the matter
axes.pole_x: taking it up, confronting or pursuing
axes.pole_y: refusing, deferring, ending or walking away
axes.definition: One side sustains or meets the situation at hand — continuing, re-examining, opposing, carrying out what was announced; the other closes it down, substitutes something else, or exits.
merged_from: s7:engagement with a demand or conflict

axes.name: concreteness
axes.definition: One side names something physically present and specifiable; the other an abstraction, a category, an attribute, a genre, a figurative use, or an evaluation of the thing.

axes.name: granularity of reference
axes.pole_x: bounded part, site or specific instance
axes.pole_y: encompassing whole, region or generic category
axes.definition: Both sides name entities of the same kind and differ in scale: a discrete part, opening, layer or narrowly specified instance against the surface, region, covering, superordinate or all-purpose term that contains it.

axes.name: register of the inner state
axes.definition: Both sides are interior, and they differ in kind: what is felt or wanted against what is known, judged, required or permitted. Sits below interiority, which separates inner from outer rather than sorting the inner.

axes.name: choice of referent within a class
axes.pole_x: one member of the referent class
axes.pole_y: another member of the same class
axes.definition: Both sides name entities of a single lexical class — body parts, garments, foodstuffs, places, times, recipients — and neither the act, the frame nor the scale differs; only which member is chosen. The residual noun axis: reach for it only when granularity, concreteness and explicitness_charge all fail to name the contrast.
merged_from: s8:referent alternation within one noun class

notes:
28 axes for 2,466 relations, inside the declared 20-40 band.

ON GROUP A AND GROUP B MEANING DIFFERENT THINGS (the question that prompted this run). Three distinct problems hide under it, and only the first is solved here.

1. Pole ORDER carries no information. "action vs speech" and "speech vs action" are one axis; sixteen readers wrote the same contrast in both orders, and folding them was the bulk of the merge. Every axis above is named for the contrast, never for a movement: `pole_x`/`pole_y` are labels, not a from/to. Nothing in this vocabulary can express "becomes abstract" — that has to be recovered later from which side lost probability, against the roster's base/aligned labels which the coders never saw.

2. Pole ASSIGNMENT is not stable across relations on the same axis, and the merge cannot fix it. A relation filed on `act_channel` tells you the contrast is verbal/physical; it does not tell you whether the base-model group was the verbal one. When these axes are applied to relations, each relation needs its poles bound to its actual two word-groups (group_a -> pole_x or pole_y) as a separate field, or direction is unrecoverable and the whole corpus collapses to "which contrasts exist" with no measurement attached. That binding is a per-relation judgement, not an axis property.

3. Some proposals were written ASYMMETRICALLY and had to be re-posed. s8's "fulfilment of the announced act" (carries out the threat / substitutes something else) and s11's "script fit" (affords the scene's activity / does not) name one pole positively and the other as its negation. I re-posed both symmetrically (engagement_vs_withdrawal, domain_specificity). Any relation whose reading survives only in the asymmetric wording will fit badly; flag rather than force it.

WHAT I COULD NOT MERGE CLEANLY.

- The four aspect-adjacent axes (event_continuity, aspectual_phase, dynamicity, act_vs_outcome) pass the one-sentence test separately but their edges touch. The discriminators: same-event-vs-different-event is continuity; where in one event's own timeline is phase; happens-vs-holds is dynamicity; doing-vs-what-the-doing-produced is act_vs_outcome. Expect coder disagreement at every seam, especially continuity/phase — s13 filed "onset of a fresh action" under phase while twelve others filed the same contrast under continuity.
- s6's "Event shape" (n=13) genuinely straddles dynamicity and valency: it bundles telicity with transitivity in one reading. Filed under dynamicity; its transitive/intransitive half belongs on valency and will have to be split by hand if the count matters.
- target_of_act is the largest merge I am least sure of (~140 relations, eighteen proposals). It absorbs three things a finer reader would separate: animacy of the target, which of two scene entities is engaged, and whether the salient object is taken up at all. Under the declared granularity rule one sentence covers all three ("one side is aimed at X, the other at Y"), so they merged; under a finer rule they are three.
- orientation_self_other versus target_of_act is a real seam that several readers crossed in both directions (s8 filed self-vs-other under "orientation of the act" with an object pole; s5's "directedness" does the same). Kept apart because "self versus another party" and "a person versus a thing" are not the same sentence.
- force_of_handling versus harm_lethality: kept separate because four readers proposed both in the same shard (s2, s11, s15 explicitly). Manner of force versus whether damage results.
- institutional_register versus domain_specificity: also a real seam. Routing an act through a legal or managerial channel is the first; marked liturgical/medical/craft vocabulary is the second. s10's "register" could sit on either; filed under domain.
- referent_substitution and syntactic_form_fit are honest residual buckets, not clean contrasts. Both are "the axis is neither semantic in the usual way nor scaled" — the first for noun slots, the second for grammaticality. Watch them: a residual bucket that grows past ~5% of the corpus is a sign that a real axis is hiding inside it.

DROPPED OR FOLDED (single-reader, low-n, judged narrower readings of something broader).
s9 "discourse relation of the continuation" (additive/contrastive connectives, n=2) into lexical_weight; s3 "discourse level" (content/metalinguistic, n=2) into lexical_weight; s9 "evaluative polarity" (n=2) into harm_lethality; s15 "Affective intensity" (acute/diffuse, n=2) into affective_vs_cognitive, which is about kind of inner state and not intensity — the one fold I am least happy with; s14 "mode of breakdown" (rupture/gradual, n=3) into force_of_handling as abruptness; s14 "sociality" (n=5) into target_of_act; s2's spatial and temporal reference (n=3 each) and s13's locative reference into referent_substitution, where deixis and calendar-versus-relative time sit uncomfortably. s9's "speech-act force" (n=2, directive/reportive) survived as illocutionary_force by joining four other readers' interrogative/declarative proposals.

WHAT I SUSPECT IS MISSING. Across the sixteen shards, ~94 relations (3.8%) were left uncovered by their own reader's axes — that residue never reached me, so any contrast that appears only there is invisible to this vocabulary by construction. Two candidates I can see edges of but cannot verify: a temporal-anchoring axis (absolute/calendar time versus deictic "next, later"), proposed once at n=3 and folded; and a quantity/measure axis (s1's degree-and-quantity words, s14's "measure of time"), which I dispersed into manner_specification and entity_vs_event rather than naming. If either shows up as systematic misfits when these axes are applied, it is the residue speaking.

PROVENANCE. `merged_from` entries are shard-prefixed proposal names (s0-s15) exactly as written by each reader, so any axis can be traced back to its sixteen wordings. Where I kept a wording I kept the clearest, not the most frequent, per the declared rule.
